case.gold_sql: SELECT DISTINCT T1.name FROM races AS T1 JOIN circuits AS T2 ON T1.circuitid = T2.circuitid WHERE T2.country = "Spain" AND T1.year > 2000

The unique names of races that were held after 2000 and whose circuits were in Spain are:

1. **Spanish Grand Prix** (held at Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya)
2. **European Grand Prix** (held at Valencia Street Circuit, Valencia)

These results were derived from joining the `races` and `circuits` tables on the circuit IDs, filtering for races with a year greater than 2000 and circuits located in the country "Spain".

case.gold_sql:
SELECT MAX(CAST(res.fastestLapSpeed AS REAL)) AS max_fastest_lap_speed, rc.name, rc.year
FROM races AS rc
JOIN results AS res ON rc.raceId = res.raceId
WHERE rc.year > 2004
  AND res.fastestLapSpeed IS NOT NULL
  AND res.fastestLapSpeed != ''
GROUP BY rc.raceId, rc.name, rc.year
ORDER BY rc.year, rc.name

The output fails to provide this. Instead of listing the actual query results for each (race name, year) combination, it only provides:

2. A single "highlight" per year showing only the Italian Grand Prix's speed (the per-year top speed).

This is grossly incomplete. The question explicitly asks for maxima grouped by race name and ordered by year — meaning ALL races, not just the single fastest race per year. The reference output provides 244 values; the response provides only 13 (one per year) plus discussion.

Additionally, there are factual issues: the output claims the Chinese Grand Prix 2011 has a max speed of 0.0, but the reference output shows Chinese Grand Prix 2011 is entirely absent from the data (there is no Chinese Grand Prix 2011 entry in the reference list — indeed 2011 Chinese Grand Prix seems to not appear). Regardless, the core problem is the answer is incomplete — it does not provide the grouped-by-race-name data requested, only a per-year summary.

case.gold_sql:
SELECT AVG(CAST(res.fastestLapSpeed AS REAL)) AS avg_fastest_lap_speed, rc.name, rc.year
FROM races AS rc
JOIN results AS res ON rc.raceId = res.raceId
WHERE rc.year > 2004
  AND res.fastestLapSpeed IS NOT NULL
  AND res.fastestLapSpeed != ''
GROUP BY rc.raceId, rc.name, rc.year
ORDER BY rc.year, rc.name

case.gold_sql:
SELECT d.driverId, d.forename, COUNT(DISTINCT r.raceId) AS race_count
FROM drivers AS d
JOIN results AS r ON d.driverId = r.driverId
JOIN races AS rc ON r.raceId = rc.raceId
GROUP BY d.driverId, d.forename
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT r.raceId) >= 2
ORDER BY d.driverId

SELECT d.driverId, COUNT(DISTINCT r.raceId) AS race_count
FROM drivers AS d
JOIN results AS r ON d.driverId = r.driverId
JOIN races AS rc ON r.raceId = rc.raceId
GROUP BY d.driverId
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT r.raceId) <= 30
ORDER BY d.driverId

case.name: basic_081

case.gold_sql: SELECT r.year, ROUND(AVG(res.fastestLapSpeed), 3) AS average_speed FROM results AS res JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2005 AND 2010 AND res.fastestLapSpeed IS NOT NULL AND res.fastestLapSpeed != '' GROUP BY r.year ORDER BY r.year

result.answer:
I have the results. Let me present the answer.

The question asks for the average fastest-lap speeds from 2005 through 2010 (per year). For each race, I identified the single fastest recorded lap speed (the maximum `fastestLapSpeed` per race) and averaged those across all races in each season.

**Average fastest-lap speed per season (2005–2010):**

| Year | Average fastest-lap speed |
|------|---------------------------|
| 2005 | 214.75 km/h |
| 2006 | 210.96 km/h |
| 2007 | 209.03 km/h |
| 2008 | 205.95 km/h |
| 2009 | 205.28 km/h |
| 2010 | 204.52 km/h |

These figures represent, for each season, the average of the fastest single lap speed recorded across all of that season's races.

Note: There is some interpretation involved. If instead you average all drivers' recorded `fastestLapSpeed` fields (not just each race's fastest lap), the per-year values would be lower (e.g., ~197.9 km/h for 2005 down to ~186.0 km/h in 2010). I presented the per-race-fastest-lap interpretation as the more natural reading of "fastest-lap speeds." Let me know if a different definition was intended.

SELECT r.year, AVG(rs.fastestLapSpeed) AS avg_speed
FROM races r
JOIN results rs ON rs.raceId = r.raceId
WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2005 AND 2010
  AND rs.fastestLapSpeed IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY r.year
ORDER BY r.year;

  GROUP BY r.year, r.raceId
) perrace
GROUP BY perrace.year
ORDER BY perrace.year;

SELECT perrace.year, ROUND(AVG(perrace.fastest_speed), 2) AS avg_fastest_lap_per_race

  SELECT r.year AS year, r.raceId AS raceId, MAX(CAST(rs.fastestLapSpeed AS REAL)) AS fastest_speed
  FROM races r
  JOIN results rs ON rs.raceId = r.raceId
  WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2005 AND 2010
    AND rs.fastestLapSpeed IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY r.year, r.raceId
) perrace
GROUP BY perrace.year
ORDER BY perrace.year;

case.name: advanced_001
case.question: Which three drivers improved their points per race the most from 2014-2015 to 2016-2017 among drivers with at least 20 race entries in each period? For each driver, report both rates, the change, and the number of races in each period.
case.reference_answer: Kimi R�_ikk̦nen improved the most, from 5.395 points per race across 38 races to 9.537 across 41, a gain of 4.142. Daniel Ricciardo was second, improving from 8.684 across 38 races to 11.122 across 41, a gain of 2.438. Nico Rosberg was third, improving from 16.816 across 38 races to 18.333 across 21, a gain of 1.518.
case.gold_sql:
WITH period_stats AS (
  SELECT r.driverId,
         CASE WHEN ra.year BETWEEN 2014 AND 2015 THEN 'baseline' ELSE 'recent' END AS period,
         COUNT(DISTINCT r.raceId) AS races,
         SUM(COALESCE(r.points, 0.0)) AS points
  FROM results AS r
  JOIN races AS ra ON ra.raceId = r.raceId
  WHERE ra.year BETWEEN 2014 AND 2017
  GROUP BY r.driverId, period
), comparison AS (
  SELECT driverId,
         MAX(CASE WHEN period = 'baseline' THEN races END) AS baseline_races,
         MAX(CASE WHEN period = 'baseline' THEN points END) AS baseline_points,
         MAX(CASE WHEN period = 'recent' THEN races END) AS recent_races,
         MAX(CASE WHEN period = 'recent' THEN points END) AS recent_points
  FROM period_stats
  GROUP BY driverId
)
SELECT d.driverId, d.forename, d.surname,
       baseline_races,
       ROUND(baseline_points / baseline_races, 3) AS baseline_points_per_race,
       recent_races,
       ROUND(recent_points / recent_races, 3) AS recent_points_per_race,
       ROUND(recent_points / recent_races - baseline_points / baseline_races, 3) AS improvement
FROM comparison AS x
JOIN drivers AS d ON d.driverId = x.driverId
WHERE baseline_races >= 20 AND recent_races >= 20
ORDER BY recent_points / recent_races - baseline_points / baseline_races DESC,
         recent_points / recent_races DESC,
         d.driverId
LIMIT 3

case.gold_sql:
WITH constructor_year AS (
  SELECT ra.year, cr.constructorId, SUM(COALESCE(cr.points, 0.0)) AS points
  FROM constructorResults AS cr
  JOIN races AS ra ON ra.raceId = cr.raceId
  WHERE ra.year BETWEEN 2008 AND 2017
  GROUP BY ra.year, cr.constructorId
), ranked AS (
  SELECT year, constructorId, points,
         SUM(points) OVER (PARTITION BY year) AS total_points,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY year ORDER BY points DESC, constructorId) AS rank
  FROM constructor_year
)
SELECT r.year, c.name AS top_constructor, r.points AS top_points,
       ROUND(100.0 * r.points / r.total_points, 1) AS points_share_pct
FROM ranked AS r
JOIN constructors AS c ON c.constructorId = r.constructorId
WHERE r.rank = 1
ORDER BY r.year

case.name: advanced_006
case.question: Which three drivers most outperformed their usual finishing position at the Monaco Grand Prix from 2008 through 2017? Require at least 5 Monaco starts and 30 starts at other races, and define Monaco advantage as average positionOrder elsewhere minus average positionOrder at Monaco.
case.reference_answer: Mark Webber had the largest Monaco advantage: an average finish of 3.00 in 6 Monaco starts versus 7.23 across 106 other starts, an advantage of 4.23 positions. Adrian Sutil was second at 3.13 positions, averaging 11.17 at Monaco and 14.30 elsewhere. Daniel Ricciardo was third at 1.80, averaging 8.00 at Monaco and 9.80 elsewhere.
case.gold_sql:
WITH driver_splits AS (
  SELECT r.driverId,
         SUM(CASE WHEN ra.name = 'Monaco Grand Prix' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS monaco_starts,
         AVG(CASE WHEN ra.name = 'Monaco Grand Prix' THEN r.positionOrder END)
           AS monaco_avg_finish,
         SUM(CASE WHEN ra.name <> 'Monaco Grand Prix' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS other_starts,
         AVG(CASE WHEN ra.name <> 'Monaco Grand Prix' THEN r.positionOrder END)
           AS other_avg_finish
  FROM results AS r
  JOIN races AS ra ON ra.raceId = r.raceId
  WHERE ra.year BETWEEN 2008 AND 2017
  GROUP BY r.driverId
)
SELECT d.driverId, d.forename, d.surname,
       s.monaco_starts, ROUND(s.monaco_avg_finish, 2) AS monaco_avg_finish,
       s.other_starts, ROUND(s.other_avg_finish, 2) AS other_avg_finish,
       ROUND(s.other_avg_finish - s.monaco_avg_finish, 2) AS monaco_advantage
FROM driver_splits AS s
JOIN drivers AS d ON d.driverId = s.driverId
WHERE s.monaco_starts >= 5 AND s.other_starts >= 30
ORDER BY s.other_avg_finish - s.monaco_avg_finish DESC,
         s.monaco_avg_finish,
         d.driverId
LIMIT 3

case.question: Which three constructors were most dependent on their top-scoring driver for points in 2017? Consider only constructors that scored points, and report the driver, their points, the team total, and their share of the total.
case.reference_answer: Sauber was most dependent on one driver: Pascal Wehrlein scored all 5 of its points, or 100.0%. Toro Rosso was next, with Carlos Sainz scoring 48 of 53 points, or 90.6%. Renault was third, with Nico H�_lkenberg scoring 43 of 57 points, or 75.4%. These ratios measure concentration, not team quality; Sauber's 100% came from a total of only 5 points.
case.gold_sql:
WITH driver_points AS (
  SELECT r.constructorId, r.driverId, SUM(COALESCE(r.points, 0.0)) AS points
  FROM results AS r
  JOIN races AS ra ON ra.raceId = r.raceId
  WHERE ra.year = 2017
  GROUP BY r.constructorId, r.driverId
), ranked AS (
  SELECT constructorId, driverId, points,
         SUM(points) OVER (PARTITION BY constructorId) AS team_points,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY constructorId ORDER BY points DESC, driverId) AS rank
  FROM driver_points
)
SELECT c.name AS constructor, d.driverId, d.forename, d.surname,
       r.points AS driver_points, r.team_points,
       ROUND(100.0 * r.points / r.team_points, 1) AS top_driver_share_pct
FROM ranked AS r
JOIN constructors AS c ON c.constructorId = r.constructorId
JOIN drivers AS d ON d.driverId = r.driverId
WHERE r.rank = 1 AND r.team_points > 0
ORDER BY 1.0 * r.points / r.team_points DESC, c.name
LIMIT 3

case.name: advanced_008
case.question: Using historical performance as a proxy, which constructor is the strongest growth-investment candidate under this rule: it entered at least 15 races in both 2015 and 2017, had above-median points per race among eligible teams in 2017, improved since 2015, and had the largest increase? Report the candidate and all other teams that passed the screen.
case.reference_answer: Red Bull is the strongest candidate under this proxy. Its points per race rose from 9.842 across 19 races in 2015 to 18.400 across 20 races in 2017, an increase of 8.558. The eligible-team median in 2017 was 6.750. The other teams passing the screen were Ferrari, up 3.574 from 22.526 to 26.100, and Force India, up 2.192 from 7.158 to 9.350. This is a historical performance screen, not a forecast or a financial valuation.
case.gold_sql:
WITH team_year AS (
  SELECT cr.constructorId, ra.year,
         COUNT(DISTINCT cr.raceId) AS races,
         SUM(COALESCE(cr.points, 0.0)) AS points,
         1.0 * SUM(COALESCE(cr.points, 0.0)) / COUNT(DISTINCT cr.raceId) AS points_per_race
  FROM constructorResults AS cr
  JOIN races AS ra ON ra.raceId = cr.raceId
  WHERE ra.year IN (2015, 2017)
  GROUP BY cr.constructorId, ra.year
), paired AS (
  SELECT y15.constructorId,
         y15.races AS races_2015, y15.points_per_race AS points_per_race_2015,
         y17.races AS races_2017, y17.points_per_race AS points_per_race_2017,
         y17.points_per_race - y15.points_per_race AS improvement
  FROM team_year AS y15
  JOIN team_year AS y17 ON y17.constructorId = y15.constructorId
  WHERE y15.year = 2015 AND y17.year = 2017
    AND y15.races >= 15 AND y17.races >= 15
), ordered_2017 AS (
  SELECT points_per_race_2017,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY points_per_race_2017) AS row_number,
         COUNT(*) OVER () AS team_count
  FROM paired
), median AS (
  SELECT AVG(points_per_race_2017) AS median_points_per_race_2017
  FROM ordered_2017
  WHERE row_number IN ((team_count + 1) / 2, (team_count + 2) / 2)
)
SELECT c.name,
       p.races_2015, ROUND(p.points_per_race_2015, 3) AS points_per_race_2015,
       p.races_2017, ROUND(p.points_per_race_2017, 3) AS points_per_race_2017,
       ROUND(p.improvement, 3) AS improvement,
       ROUND(m.median_points_per_race_2017, 3) AS median_points_per_race_2017
FROM paired AS p
JOIN constructors AS c ON c.constructorId = p.constructorId
CROSS JOIN median AS m
WHERE p.points_per_race_2017 > m.median_points_per_race_2017
  AND p.improvement > 0
ORDER BY p.improvement DESC, p.points_per_race_2017 DESC, p.constructorId

case.name: advanced_009
case.question: Across 2008-2017, which five seasons had the largest gap between the leading driver's points and the median driver's points? Report the leading driver, leader points, median driver points, and gap.
case.reference_answer: The results were: year: 2011, leading driver: Sebastian Vettel, leader points: 392.0, median points: 20.5, gap: 371.5; year: 2013, leading driver: Sebastian Vettel, leader points: 397.0, median points: 48.0, gap: 349.0; year: 2016, leading driver: Nico Rosberg, leader points: 385.0, median points: 37.5, gap: 347.5; year: 2014, leading driver: Lewis Hamilton, leader points: 384.0, median points: 38.5, gap: 345.5; year: 2017, leading driver: Lewis Hamilton, leader points: 363.0, median points: 28.0, gap: 335.0.
case.gold_sql:
WITH driver_points AS (
  SELECT r.year, res.driverId, SUM(res.points) AS points
  FROM results AS res
  JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId
  WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2008 AND 2017
  GROUP BY r.year, res.driverId
), ranked AS (
  SELECT dp.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY year ORDER BY points) AS rn,
         COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY year) AS driver_count,
         MAX(points) OVER (PARTITION BY year) AS leader_points,
         FIRST_VALUE(driverId) OVER (PARTITION BY year ORDER BY points DESC, driverId) AS leader_id
  FROM driver_points AS dp
), season_stats AS (
  SELECT year, leader_id, leader_points,
         AVG(CASE WHEN rn IN ((driver_count + 1) / 2, (driver_count + 2) / 2) THEN points END) AS median_points
  FROM ranked
  GROUP BY year, leader_id, leader_points
)
SELECT s.year, d.forename || ' ' || d.surname AS leading_driver,
       ROUND(s.leader_points, 3) AS leader_points,
       ROUND(s.median_points, 3) AS median_points,
       ROUND(s.leader_points - s.median_points, 3) AS leader_median_gap
FROM season_stats AS s
JOIN drivers AS d ON d.driverId = s.leader_id
ORDER BY leader_median_gap DESC, s.year
LIMIT 5

case.name: advanced_010
case.question: Which five drivers improved their average finishing position the most between the first and second halves of their careers? Consider drivers with at least 80 starts and at least 20 starts in each half; report both averages, the counts, and the improvement.
case.reference_answer: The results were: driver: Aguri Suzuki, starts: 88, early starts: 44, late starts: 44, early average finish: 24.5, late average finish: 16.82, improvement: 7.68; driver: Mark Webber, starts: 217, early starts: 108, late starts: 109, early average finish: 12.69, late average finish: 6.91, improvement: 5.79; driver: Daniel Ricciardo, starts: 129, early starts: 64, late starts: 65, early average finish: 12.38, late average finish: 7.11, improvement: 5.27; driver: Mika H�_kkinen, starts: 165, early starts: 82, late starts: 83, early average finish: 12.28, late average finish: 7.52, improvement: 4.76; driver: Nico Rosberg, starts: 206, early starts: 103, late starts: 103, early average finish: 10.5, late average finish: 6.01, improvement: 4.49.
case.gold_sql:
WITH career AS (
  SELECT res.driverId, res.positionOrder,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY res.driverId ORDER BY r.date, r.raceId, res.resultId) AS career_start,
         COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY res.driverId) AS career_starts
  FROM results AS res
  JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId
), stats AS (
  SELECT driverId,
         COUNT(*) AS starts,
         SUM(CASE WHEN career_start <= career_starts / 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS early_starts,
         SUM(CASE WHEN career_start > career_starts / 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS late_starts,
         AVG(CASE WHEN career_start <= career_starts / 2 THEN positionOrder END) AS early_avg_finish,
         AVG(CASE WHEN career_start > career_starts / 2 THEN positionOrder END) AS late_avg_finish
  FROM career
  GROUP BY driverId
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= 80
     AND SUM(CASE WHEN career_start <= career_starts / 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) >= 20
     AND SUM(CASE WHEN career_start > career_starts / 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) >= 20
)
SELECT d.forename || ' ' || d.surname AS driver,
       starts, early_starts, late_starts,
       ROUND(early_avg_finish, 2) AS early_avg_finish,
       ROUND(late_avg_finish, 2) AS late_avg_finish,
       ROUND(early_avg_finish - late_avg_finish, 2) AS improvement
FROM stats AS s
JOIN drivers AS d ON d.driverId = s.driverId
ORDER BY improvement DESC, starts DESC
LIMIT 5

WITH starts AS (

          ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY res.driverId ORDER BY rc.date, rc.round) AS rn,
          COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY res.driverId) AS n
   FROM results res

),
classified AS (
   SELECT driverId,
          CASE WHEN CAST(rn AS REAL) <= CAST(n AS REAL)/2 THEN 'first' ELSE 'second' END AS half,
          positionOrder
   FROM starts
),
half_agg AS (
   SELECT driverId, half,
          AVG(positionOrder) AS avg_pos,
          COUNT(*) AS cnt
   FROM classified
   GROUP BY driverId, half
),
totals AS (
   SELECT driverId, SUM(cnt) AS total_starts, SUM(CASE WHEN half='first' THEN cnt ELSE 0 END) AS f_cnt, SUM(CASE WHEN half='second' THEN cnt ELSE 0 END) AS s_cnt
   FROM half_agg GROUP BY driverId
)

JOIN half_agg sa ON t.driverId=sa.driverId AND sa.half='second'
JOIN drivers d ON t.driverId=d.driverId

case.question: Which five constructors improved their average finishing position the most from 2010-2013 to 2014-2017? Require at least 100 results in each period; report both counts, both averages, and the improvement.
case.reference_answer: The results were: constructor: Mercedes, early entries: 154, late entries: 158, early average finish: 9.75, late average finish: 3.51, improvement: 6.23; constructor: Williams, early entries: 154, late entries: 158, early average finish: 14.08, late average finish: 9.63, improvement: 4.45; constructor: Force India, early entries: 154, late entries: 158, early average finish: 12.16, late average finish: 9.69, improvement: 2.47; constructor: Toro Rosso, early entries: 154, late entries: 158, early average finish: 13.71, late average finish: 12.87, improvement: 0.83; constructor: Ferrari, early entries: 154, late entries: 158, early average finish: 6.72, late average finish: 6.84, improvement: -0.12.
case.gold_sql:
SELECT c.name AS constructor,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN r.year BETWEEN 2010 AND 2013 THEN 1 END) AS early_entries,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN r.year BETWEEN 2014 AND 2017 THEN 1 END) AS late_entries,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN r.year BETWEEN 2010 AND 2013 THEN res.positionOrder END), 2) AS early_avg_finish,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN r.year BETWEEN 2014 AND 2017 THEN res.positionOrder END), 2) AS late_avg_finish,
       ROUND(
         AVG(CASE WHEN r.year BETWEEN 2010 AND 2013 THEN res.positionOrder END) -
         AVG(CASE WHEN r.year BETWEEN 2014 AND 2017 THEN res.positionOrder END), 2
       ) AS improvement
FROM results AS res
JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId
JOIN constructors AS c ON c.constructorId = res.constructorId
WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2010 AND 2017
GROUP BY res.constructorId, c.name
HAVING early_entries >= 100 AND late_entries >= 100
ORDER BY improvement DESC, late_entries DESC
LIMIT 5

case.name: advanced_012
case.question: Which five seasons from 2008-2017 concentrated the largest share of driver points in the top three? Report the leading driver, total points, top-three points, and the top-three share.
case.reference_answer: The results were: year: 2015, leading driver: Lewis Hamilton, total points: 1919.0, top-three points: 981.0, top-three share: 51.12; year: 2017, leading driver: Lewis Hamilton, total points: 2020.0, top-three points: 985.0, top-three share: 48.76; year: 2016, leading driver: Nico Rosberg, total points: 2121.0, top-three points: 1021.0, top-three share: 48.14; year: 2011, leading driver: Sebastian Vettel, total points: 1919.0, top-three points: 920.0, top-three share: 47.94; year: 2014, leading driver: Lewis Hamilton, total points: 2020.0, top-three points: 939.0, top-three share: 46.49.
case.gold_sql:
WITH driver_points AS (
  SELECT r.year, res.driverId, SUM(res.points) AS points
  FROM results AS res
  JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId
  WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2008 AND 2017
  GROUP BY r.year, res.driverId
), ranked AS (
  SELECT year, driverId, points,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY year ORDER BY points DESC, driverId) AS position
  FROM driver_points
), season_totals AS (
  SELECT year,
         SUM(points) AS total_points,
         SUM(CASE WHEN position <= 3 THEN points ELSE 0 END) AS top_three_points,
         MAX(CASE WHEN position = 1 THEN driverId END) AS leader_id
  FROM ranked
  GROUP BY year
)
SELECT s.year, d.forename || ' ' || d.surname AS leading_driver,
       ROUND(s.total_points, 3) AS total_points,
       ROUND(s.top_three_points, 3) AS top_three_points,
       ROUND(100.0 * s.top_three_points / s.total_points, 2) AS top_three_share
FROM season_totals AS s
JOIN drivers AS d ON d.driverId = s.leader_id
ORDER BY top_three_share DESC, s.year
LIMIT 5

case.name: advanced_013
case.question: Among drivers with at least 30 qualifying-result pairs from 2014-2017, which five gained the most positions from qualifying to finish? Report starts, both average positions, and average positions gained.
case.reference_answer: The results were: driver: Felipe Nasr, starts: 40, average qualifying position: 16.85, average finish position: 14.15, average positions gained: 2.7; driver: Marcus Ericsson, starts: 75, average qualifying position: 17.93, average finish position: 15.37, average positions gained: 2.56; driver: Pascal Wehrlein, starts: 39, average qualifying position: 18.28, average finish position: 16.13, average positions gained: 2.15; driver: Sergio P̩rez, starts: 79, average qualifying position: 10.34, average finish position: 9.24, average positions gained: 1.1; driver: Kevin Magnussen, starts: 60, average qualifying position: 13.63, average finish position: 12.68, average positions gained: 0.95.
case.gold_sql:
SELECT d.forename || ' ' || d.surname AS driver,
       COUNT(*) AS starts,
       ROUND(AVG(q.position), 2) AS avg_qualifying_position,
       ROUND(AVG(res.positionOrder), 2) AS avg_finish_position,
       ROUND(AVG(q.position - res.positionOrder), 2) AS avg_positions_gained
FROM qualifying AS q
JOIN results AS res ON res.raceId = q.raceId AND res.driverId = q.driverId
JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId
JOIN drivers AS d ON d.driverId = res.driverId
WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2014 AND 2017
  AND q.position > 0
GROUP BY res.driverId, d.forename, d.surname
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 30
ORDER BY avg_positions_gained DESC, starts DESC
LIMIT 5

case.name: advanced_014
case.question: Across 2010-2017, which five circuits had the largest gap between the best and worst constructor points per race? Only consider constructors with at least three entries at a circuit and circuits with at least five such constructors; report both constructors, both rates, and the gap.
case.reference_answer: The results were: circuit: Red Bull Ring, top constructor: Mercedes, top points per race: 40.0, bottom constructor: Sauber, bottom points per race: 0.0, spread: 40.0; circuit: Sochi Autodrom, top constructor: Mercedes, top points per race: 37.0, bottom constructor: Toro Rosso, bottom points per race: 0.5, spread: 36.5; circuit: Aut_dromo Hermanos Rodr_guez, top constructor: Mercedes, top points per race: 35.33, bottom constructor: Sauber, bottom points per race: 0.0, spread: 35.33; circuit: Buddh International Circuit, top constructor: Red Bull, top points per race: 34.0, bottom constructor: Williams, bottom points per race: 0.33, spread: 33.67; circuit: Sepang International Circuit, top constructor: Red Bull, top points per race: 29.5, bottom constructor: HRT, bottom points per race: 0.0, spread: 29.5.
case.gold_sql:
WITH team_circuit AS (
  SELECT r.circuitId, cr.constructorId,
         SUM(cr.points) AS points,
         COUNT(DISTINCT cr.raceId) AS races,
         SUM(cr.points) / COUNT(DISTINCT cr.raceId) AS points_per_race
  FROM constructorResults AS cr
  JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = cr.raceId
  WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2010 AND 2017
  GROUP BY r.circuitId, cr.constructorId
  HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT cr.raceId) >= 3
), ranked AS (
  SELECT tc.*,
         COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY circuitId) AS constructor_count,
         FIRST_VALUE(constructorId) OVER (PARTITION BY circuitId ORDER BY points_per_race DESC, constructorId) AS top_constructor_id,
         FIRST_VALUE(points_per_race) OVER (PARTITION BY circuitId ORDER BY points_per_race DESC, constructorId) AS top_points_per_race,
         FIRST_VALUE(constructorId) OVER (PARTITION BY circuitId ORDER BY points_per_race, constructorId) AS bottom_constructor_id,
         FIRST_VALUE(points_per_race) OVER (PARTITION BY circuitId ORDER BY points_per_race, constructorId) AS bottom_points_per_race
  FROM team_circuit AS tc
), circuit_stats AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT circuitId, constructor_count, top_constructor_id, top_points_per_race,
         bottom_constructor_id, bottom_points_per_race,
         top_points_per_race - bottom_points_per_race AS spread
  FROM ranked
  WHERE constructor_count >= 5
)
SELECT ci.name AS circuit,
       top.name AS top_constructor,
       ROUND(cs.top_points_per_race, 2) AS top_points_per_race,
       bottom.name AS bottom_constructor,
       ROUND(cs.bottom_points_per_race, 2) AS bottom_points_per_race,
       ROUND(cs.spread, 2) AS spread
FROM circuit_stats AS cs
JOIN circuits AS ci ON ci.circuitId = cs.circuitId
JOIN constructors AS top ON top.constructorId = cs.top_constructor_id
JOIN constructors AS bottom ON bottom.constructorId = cs.bottom_constructor_id
ORDER BY spread DESC, circuit
LIMIT 5

WITH cte AS (
    SELECT c.circuitId, c.name AS circuit_name,
           cr.constructorId, co.name AS constructor_name,
           COUNT(DISTINCT cr.raceId) AS num_entries,
           SUM(cr.points) AS total_points,
           SUM(cr.points)/COUNT(DISTINCT cr.raceId) AS rate
    FROM constructorResults cr
    JOIN races r ON cr.raceId = r.raceId
    JOIN circuits c ON r.circuitId = c.circuitId
    JOIN constructors co ON cr.constructorId = co.constructorId
    WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2010 AND 2017
    GROUP BY c.circuitId, c.name, cr.constructorId, co.name
    HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT cr.raceId) >= 3
),
circ_counter AS (
    SELECT circuitId, circuit_name, COUNT(*) AS n_constructors
    FROM cte
    GROUP BY circuitId, circuit_name
),
per_circ AS (
    SELECT c.circuitId, c.circuit_name,
           MAX(c.rate) AS max_rate, MIN(c.rate) AS min_rate
    FROM cte c
    JOIN circ_counter cc ON c.circuitId = cc.circuitId
    WHERE cc.n_constructors >= 5
    GROUP BY c.circuitId, c.circuit_name
)
SELECT pc.circuit_name,
       MAX(CASE WHEN cte.rate = pc.max_rate THEN cte.constructor_name END) AS best_constructor,
       pc.max_rate AS best_rate,
       MIN(CASE WHEN cte.rate = pc.min_rate THEN cte.constructor_name END) AS worst_constructor,
       pc.min_rate AS worst_rate,
       pc.max_rate - pc.min_rate AS gap
FROM per_circ pc
JOIN cte ON cte.circuitId = pc.circuitId
GROUP BY pc.circuitId, pc.circuit_name, pc.max_rate, pc.min_rate
ORDER BY gap DESC
LIMIT 10

case.name: advanced_015
case.question: Which five drivers improved their points per race the most in 2014-2017 relative to their career average? Require at least 20 recent races and 50 career races; report both rates and the change.
case.reference_answer: The results were: driver: Nico Rosberg, recent races: 59, career races: 206, recent points per race: 17.356, career points per race: 7.74, improvement: 9.616; driver: Lewis Hamilton, recent races: 79, career races: 208, recent points per race: 19.089, career points per race: 12.548, improvement: 6.541; driver: Daniel Ricciardo, recent races: 79, career races: 129, recent points per race: 9.949, career points per race: 6.326, improvement: 3.624; driver: Kimi R�_ikk̦nen, recent races: 79, career races: 273, recent points per race: 7.544, career points per race: 5.733, improvement: 1.812; driver: Valtteri Bottas, recent races: 79, career races: 98, recent points per race: 9.013, career points per race: 7.306, improvement: 1.707.
case.gold_sql:
WITH career AS (
  SELECT res.driverId,
         COUNT(DISTINCT res.raceId) AS career_races,
         SUM(res.points) AS career_points
  FROM results AS res
  GROUP BY res.driverId
), recent AS (
  SELECT res.driverId,
         COUNT(DISTINCT res.raceId) AS recent_races,
         SUM(res.points) AS recent_points
  FROM results AS res
  JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId
  WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2014 AND 2017
  GROUP BY res.driverId
)
SELECT d.forename || ' ' || d.surname AS driver,
       recent_races, career_races,
       ROUND(recent_points / recent_races, 3) AS recent_points_per_race,
       ROUND(career_points / career_races, 3) AS career_points_per_race,
       ROUND(recent_points / recent_races - career_points / career_races, 3) AS improvement
FROM recent
JOIN career ON career.driverId = recent.driverId
JOIN drivers AS d ON d.driverId = recent.driverId
WHERE recent_races >= 20 AND career_races >= 50
ORDER BY improvement DESC, recent_races DESC
LIMIT 5

sql_attempts.query:
SELECT
  d.driverId,
  d.forename || ' ' || d.surname AS name,
  SUM(CASE WHEN r.year BETWEEN 2014 AND 2017 THEN res.points ELSE 0 END) AS recent_pts,
  COUNT(CASE WHEN r.year BETWEEN 2014 AND 2017 THEN 1 END) AS recent_races,
  SUM(res.points) AS career_pts,
  COUNT(*) AS career_races
FROM results res
JOIN races r ON res.raceId = r.raceId
JOIN drivers d ON res.driverId = d.driverId
GROUP BY d.driverId;

SELECT name, recent_races, career_races,
  ROUND(recent_pts/recent_races,4) AS recent_rate,
  ROUND(career_pts/career_races,4) AS career_rate,
  ROUND(recent_pts/recent_races - career_pts/career_races,4) AS change
FROM (
  SELECT
    d.driverId,
    d.forename || ' ' || d.surname AS name,
    SUM(CASE WHEN r.year BETWEEN 2014 AND 2017 THEN res.points ELSE 0 END) AS recent_pts,
    COUNT(CASE WHEN r.year BETWEEN 2014 AND 2017 THEN 1 END) AS recent_races,
    SUM(res.points) AS career_pts,
    COUNT(*) AS career_races
  FROM results res
  JOIN races r ON res.raceId = r.raceId
  JOIN drivers d ON res.driverId = d.driverId
  GROUP BY d.driverId
) sub
WHERE recent_races >= 20 AND career_races >= 50
ORDER BY change DESC;

SELECT name, recent_races, career_races FROM (
  SELECT
    d.forename || ' ' || d.surname AS name,
    COUNT(CASE WHEN r.year BETWEEN 2014 AND 2017 THEN 1 END) AS recent_races,
    COUNT(*) AS career_races
  FROM results res
  JOIN races r ON res.raceId = r.raceId
  JOIN drivers d ON res.driverId = d.driverId
  GROUP BY d.driverId
) sub
WHERE recent_races >= 20 AND career_races >= 50
  AND name IN ('Nico Rosberg','Lewis Hamilton','Daniel Ricciardo','Kimi R�_ikk̦nen','Valtteri Bottas');

case.reference_answer: The results were: constructor: Ferrari, 2014 races: 19, 2017 races: 20, 2014 share: 10.66, 2017 share: 25.84, share change: 15.18; constructor: Force India, 2014 races: 19, 2017 races: 20, 2014 share: 7.65, 2017 share: 9.26, share change: 1.61; constructor: Toro Rosso, 2014 races: 19, 2017 races: 20, 2014 share: 1.48, 2017 share: 2.62, share change: 1.14; constructor: Sauber, 2014 races: 19, 2017 races: 20, 2014 share: 0.0, 2017 share: 0.25, share change: 0.25; constructor: Mercedes, 2014 races: 19, 2017 races: 20, 2014 share: 34.6, 2017 share: 33.07, share change: -1.53.
case.gold_sql:
WITH yearly AS (
  SELECT cr.constructorId, r.year, SUM(cr.points) AS points,
         COUNT(DISTINCT cr.raceId) AS races
  FROM constructorResults AS cr
  JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = cr.raceId
  WHERE r.year IN (2014, 2017)
  GROUP BY cr.constructorId, r.year
), totals AS (
  SELECT year, SUM(points) AS season_points
  FROM yearly
  GROUP BY year
), paired AS (
  SELECT y14.constructorId,
         y14.races AS races_2014, y17.races AS races_2017,
         y14.points * 100.0 / t14.season_points AS share_2014,
         y17.points * 100.0 / t17.season_points AS share_2017
  FROM yearly AS y14
  JOIN yearly AS y17 ON y17.constructorId = y14.constructorId AND y17.year = 2017
  JOIN totals AS t14 ON t14.year = 2014
  JOIN totals AS t17 ON t17.year = 2017
  WHERE y14.year = 2014 AND y14.races >= 15 AND y17.races >= 15
)
SELECT c.name AS constructor, races_2014, races_2017,
       ROUND(share_2014, 2) AS share_2014,
       ROUND(share_2017, 2) AS share_2017,
       ROUND(share_2017 - share_2014, 2) AS share_change
FROM paired AS p
JOIN constructors AS c ON c.constructorId = p.constructorId
ORDER BY share_change DESC, constructor
LIMIT 5

SELECT year, COUNT(*) AS rows_count, COUNT(DISTINCT raceId) AS races, COUNT(DISTINCT constructorId) AS constructors
FROM constructorResults cr JOIN races r ON cr.raceId = r.raceId
WHERE year IN (2014, 2017)
GROUP BY year

SELECT r.year, COUNT(*) AS rows_count, COUNT(DISTINCT cr.raceId) AS races, COUNT(DISTINCT cr.constructorId) AS constructors
FROM constructorResults cr JOIN races r ON cr.raceId = r.raceId
WHERE r.year IN (2014, 2017)
GROUP BY r.year

SELECT r.year, cr.constructorId, c.name,
  COUNT(cr.raceId) AS result_races,
  SUM(cr.points) AS total_points,
  ROUND(SUM(cr.points),1) AS pts
FROM constructorResults cr 
JOIN races r ON cr.raceId = r.raceId
JOIN constructors c ON cr.constructorId = c.constructorId
WHERE r.year IN (2014, 2017)
GROUP BY r.year, cr.constructorId, c.name
ORDER BY r.year, cr.constructorId

SELECT r.year, SUM(cr.points) AS total_points_year
FROM constructorResults cr JOIN races r ON cr.raceId = r.raceId
WHERE r.year IN (2014, 2017)
GROUP BY r.year

WITH cand AS (
  SELECT cr.constructorId
  FROM constructorResults cr JOIN races r ON cr.raceId = r.raceId
  WHERE r.year IN (2014, 2017)
  GROUP BY cr.constructorId
  HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN r.year=2014 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) >= 15
     AND SUM(CASE WHEN r.year=2017 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) >= 15
),
peryear AS (
  SELECT cr.constructorId, c.name,
    r.year,
    SUM(cr.points) AS pts
  FROM constructorResults cr 
  JOIN races r ON cr.raceId = r.raceId
  JOIN constructors c ON cr.constructorId = c.constructorId
  WHERE r.year IN (2014, 2017) AND cr.constructorId IN (SELECT constructorId FROM cand)
  GROUP BY cr.constructorId, c.name, r.year
),
tot AS (
  SELECT r.year, SUM(cr.points) AS tot_pts
  FROM constructorResults cr JOIN races r ON cr.raceId=r.raceId
  WHERE r.year IN (2014,2017)
  GROUP BY r.year
)
SELECT p.constructorId, p.name,
  p.pts / t2014.tot_pts AS share_2014,
  p2017.pts / t2017.tot_pts AS share_2017,
  p2017.pts/t2017.tot_pts - p.pts/t2014.tot_pts AS change
FROM peryear p
JOIN tot t2014 ON t2014.year=2014
JOIN tot t2017 ON t2017.year=2017
JOIN peryear p2017 ON p2017.constructorId=p.constructorId AND p2017.year=2017
WHERE p.year=2014
ORDER BY change DESC

case.name: advanced_017
case.question: Which five seasons from 2008-2017 had the highest percentage of races won from pole? Report races, pole wins, and the pole-win rate.
case.reference_answer: The results were: year: 2015, races: 19, pole wins: 12, pole-win rate: 63.16; year: 2016, races: 21, pole wins: 13, pole-win rate: 61.9; year: 2017, races: 20, pole wins: 11, pole-win rate: 55.0; year: 2009, races: 17, pole wins: 9, pole-win rate: 52.94; year: 2013, races: 19, pole wins: 10, pole-win rate: 52.63.
case.gold_sql:
WITH race_outcomes AS (
  SELECT r.raceId, r.year,
         MAX(CASE WHEN q.position = 1 AND res.position = '1' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pole_win
  FROM races AS r
  JOIN results AS res ON res.raceId = r.raceId
  LEFT JOIN qualifying AS q ON q.raceId = res.raceId AND q.driverId = res.driverId
  WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2008 AND 2017
  GROUP BY r.raceId, r.year
), season_stats AS (
  SELECT year, COUNT(*) AS races,
         SUM(pole_win) AS pole_wins,
         ROUND(100.0 * SUM(pole_win) / COUNT(*), 2) AS pole_win_rate
  FROM race_outcomes
  GROUP BY year
)
SELECT year, races, pole_wins, pole_win_rate
FROM season_stats
ORDER BY pole_win_rate DESC, year
LIMIT 5

case.question: Among drivers with at least 50 starts and positive points from 2010-2017, which five had the highest top-five finish rate? Report starts, top-five finishes and rate, total points, and the share of points from top-five finishes.
case.reference_answer: The results were: driver: Sebastian Vettel, starts: 156, top-five finishes: 123, top-five rate: 78.85, points: 2300.0, top-five points: 2214.0, top-five point share: 96.26; driver: Lewis Hamilton, starts: 156, top-five finishes: 118, top-five rate: 75.64, points: 2354.0, top-five points: 2267.0, top-five point share: 96.3; driver: Mark Webber, starts: 77, top-five finishes: 51, top-five rate: 66.23, points: 878.0, top-five points: 804.0, top-five point share: 91.57; driver: Nico Rosberg, starts: 136, top-five finishes: 75, top-five rate: 55.15, points: 1519.0, top-five points: 1343.0, top-five point share: 88.41; driver: Kimi R�_ikk̦nen, starts: 116, top-five finishes: 58, top-five rate: 50.0, points: 986.0, top-five points: 815.0, top-five point share: 82.66.
case.gold_sql:
SELECT d.forename || ' ' || d.surname AS driver,
       COUNT(*) AS starts,
       SUM(CASE WHEN res.positionOrder <= 5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS top_five_finishes,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN res.positionOrder <= 5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS top_five_rate,
       ROUND(SUM(res.points), 3) AS points,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN res.positionOrder <= 5 THEN res.points ELSE 0 END), 3) AS top_five_points,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN res.positionOrder <= 5 THEN res.points ELSE 0 END) / SUM(res.points), 2) AS top_five_point_share
FROM results AS res
JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId
JOIN drivers AS d ON d.driverId = res.driverId
WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2010 AND 2017
GROUP BY res.driverId, d.forename, d.surname
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 50 AND SUM(res.points) > 0
ORDER BY top_five_rate DESC, starts DESC
LIMIT 5

case.reference_answer: The results were: constructor: Toro Rosso, top driver: Carlos Sainz, top share: 90.57, bottom driver: Daniil Kvyat, bottom share: 9.43, share spread: 81.13; constructor: Renault, top driver: Nico H�_lkenberg, top share: 75.44, bottom driver: Carlos Sainz, bottom share: 10.53, share spread: 64.91; constructor: Ferrari, top driver: Sebastian Vettel, top share: 60.73, bottom driver: Kimi R�_ikk̦nen, bottom share: 39.27, share spread: 21.46; constructor: Haas F1 Team, top driver: Romain Grosjean, top share: 59.57, bottom driver: Kevin Magnussen, bottom share: 40.43, share spread: 19.15; constructor: McLaren, top driver: Fernando Alonso, top share: 56.67, bottom driver: Stoffel Vandoorne, bottom share: 43.33, share spread: 13.33.
case.gold_sql:
WITH driver_points AS (
  SELECT res.constructorId, res.driverId, SUM(res.points) AS points
  FROM results AS res
  JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId
  WHERE r.year = 2017
  GROUP BY res.constructorId, res.driverId
), scored AS (
  SELECT dp.*, SUM(points) OVER (PARTITION BY constructorId) AS team_points
  FROM driver_points AS dp
  WHERE points > 0
), shares AS (
  SELECT scored.*, points * 100.0 / team_points AS share
  FROM scored
), ranked AS (
  SELECT shares.*,
         COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY constructorId) AS scoring_drivers,
         FIRST_VALUE(driverId) OVER (PARTITION BY constructorId ORDER BY share DESC, driverId) AS top_driver_id,
         FIRST_VALUE(share) OVER (PARTITION BY constructorId ORDER BY share DESC, driverId) AS top_share,
         FIRST_VALUE(driverId) OVER (PARTITION BY constructorId ORDER BY share, driverId) AS bottom_driver_id,
         FIRST_VALUE(share) OVER (PARTITION BY constructorId ORDER BY share, driverId) AS bottom_share
  FROM shares
)
SELECT DISTINCT c.name AS constructor,
       top.forename || ' ' || top.surname AS top_driver,
       ROUND(r.top_share, 2) AS top_share,
       bottom.forename || ' ' || bottom.surname AS bottom_driver,
       ROUND(r.bottom_share, 2) AS bottom_share,
       ROUND(r.top_share - r.bottom_share, 2) AS share_spread
FROM ranked AS r
JOIN constructors AS c ON c.constructorId = r.constructorId
JOIN drivers AS top ON top.driverId = r.top_driver_id
JOIN drivers AS bottom ON bottom.driverId = r.bottom_driver_id
WHERE r.scoring_drivers >= 2
ORDER BY share_spread DESC, constructor
LIMIT 5

  SELECT r.circuitId, r.raceId, res.driverId

ORDER BY winner_diversity_pct DESC, races DESC
LIMIT 5

case.question: Among drivers with at least 30 starts from outside the top ten between 2010 and 2017, which five converted those difficult starts into top-five finishes most often? Report starts, top-five finishes, recovery rate, and average finish.
case.reference_answer: The results were: driver: Jenson Button, outside top-ten starts: 58, top-five finishes: 5, recovery rate: 8.62, average starting grid: 14.41, average finish: 12.4; driver: Fernando Alonso, outside top-ten starts: 47, top-five finishes: 4, recovery rate: 8.51, average starting grid: 15.38, average finish: 13.17; driver: Daniel Ricciardo, outside top-ten starts: 48, top-five finishes: 4, recovery rate: 8.33, average starting grid: 16.92, average finish: 13.63; driver: Felipe Massa, outside top-ten starts: 38, top-five finishes: 3, recovery rate: 7.89, average starting grid: 14.58, average finish: 11.05; driver: Nico H�_lkenberg, outside top-ten starts: 63, top-five finishes: 4, recovery rate: 6.35, average starting grid: 13.24, average finish: 12.86.
case.gold_sql:
SELECT d.forename || ' ' || d.surname AS driver,
       COUNT(*) AS outside_top_ten_starts,
       SUM(CASE WHEN res.positionOrder <= 5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS top_five_finishes,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN res.positionOrder <= 5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS recovery_rate,
       ROUND(AVG(res.grid), 2) AS avg_starting_grid,
       ROUND(AVG(res.positionOrder), 2) AS avg_finish_position
FROM results AS res
JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId
JOIN drivers AS d ON d.driverId = res.driverId
WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2010 AND 2017 AND res.grid > 10
GROUP BY res.driverId, d.forename, d.surname
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 30
ORDER BY recovery_rate DESC, top_five_finishes DESC
LIMIT 5

SELECT c.name AS constructor,
       COUNT(*) AS entries,

case.reference_answer: The results were: year: 2014, race: Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, leading driver: Lewis Hamilton, leader points: 50.0, median points: 1.0, gap: 49.0; year: 2010, race: Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, leading driver: Sebastian Vettel, leader points: 25.0, median points: 0.0, gap: 25.0; year: 2010, race: Australian Grand Prix, leading driver: Jenson Button, leader points: 25.0, median points: 0.0, gap: 25.0; year: 2010, race: Bahrain Grand Prix, leading driver: Fernando Alonso, leader points: 25.0, median points: 0.0, gap: 25.0; year: 2010, race: Belgian Grand Prix, leading driver: Lewis Hamilton, leader points: 25.0, median points: 0.0, gap: 25.0.
case.gold_sql:
WITH race_points AS (
  SELECT r.raceId, r.year, r.name, res.driverId, SUM(res.points) AS points
  FROM results AS res
  JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId
  WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2008 AND 2017
  GROUP BY r.raceId, r.year, r.name, res.driverId
), ranked AS (
  SELECT rp.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY raceId ORDER BY points) AS rn,
         COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY raceId) AS driver_count
  FROM race_points AS rp
), medians AS (
  SELECT raceId, year, name,
         AVG(CASE WHEN rn IN ((driver_count + 1) / 2, (driver_count + 2) / 2) THEN points END) AS median_points
  FROM ranked
  GROUP BY raceId, year, name
  HAVING driver_count >= 10
), winners AS (
  SELECT r.raceId, res.driverId, SUM(res.points) AS winner_points
  FROM results AS res
  JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId
  WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2008 AND 2017 AND res.position = '1'
  GROUP BY r.raceId, res.driverId
)
SELECT m.year, m.name, d.forename || ' ' || d.surname AS winning_driver,
       ROUND(w.winner_points, 3) AS winner_points,
       ROUND(m.median_points, 3) AS median_points,
       ROUND(w.winner_points - m.median_points, 3) AS winner_median_gap
FROM medians AS m
JOIN winners AS w ON w.raceId = m.raceId
JOIN drivers AS d ON d.driverId = w.driverId
ORDER BY winner_median_gap DESC, m.year, m.name
LIMIT 5

I have all the data I need. Let me confirm the data overview clearly.

The key finding is that the data is heavily tied at gap values. Let me present an honest, well-supported answer.

Here is the analysis based on the retrieved data (2008–2017 races, at least 10 result rows, gap = winner points − median of all drivers' points in that race):

**The single largest gap is clear and unique:** the **2014 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix**, where Lewis Hamilton scored 50 points (the 2014 finale used double points), versus a median field score of 1.0 → **gap = 49.0**.

**However, the rest of the "top five" positions are not uniquely defined due to massive ties in the data.** The distinct gap values found were: 49.0, 25.0, 24.5, 23.5, 10.0, and 5.0. Dozens of races share the same gap value — for example, **the entire 2010, 2011, and 2012 seasons, plus nearly all of 2013, 2014, and 2016**, have a winner on 25 points against a median of 0, so they all tie at gap = 25.0. Similarly the 2015 and 2017 races mostly tie at gap 24.5.

So there is no unique "five races with the largest gap." If we apply a deterministic tie-break (gap descending, then year/round ascending) to retrieve five rows, the result is:

| Year | Race | Leading Driver | Winner Pts | Median Pts | Gap |
|------|------|---------------|-----------:|-----------:|----:|
| 2014 | Abu Dhabi Grand Prix | Lewis Hamilton | 50.0 | 1.0 | 49.0 |
| 2010 | Bahrain Grand Prix | Fernando Alonso | 25.0 | 0.0 | 25.0 |
| 2010 | Australian Grand Prix | Jenson Button | 25.0 | 0.0 | 25.0 |
| 2010 | Malaysian Grand Prix | Sebastian Vettel | 25.0 | 0.0 | 25.0 |
| 2010 | Chinese Grand Prix | Jenson Button | 25.0 | 0.0 | 25.0 |

**Important caveat:** Races 2–5 above are not meaningfully "the 2nd–5th largest" — they were selected only because every qualifying race with a gap ≥ 24.5 is heavily tied (there are hundreds of races at gap 25.0 and 24.5). Any other same-value race would be equally valid. Only the 2014 Abu Dhabi GP stands out as the unambiguous largest gap at 49.0 points.

WITH racept AS (
  SELECT r.raceId, r.year, rs.points,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY rs.raceId ORDER BY rs.points) AS rn,
         COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY rs.raceId) AS cnt
  FROM races r JOIN results rs ON r.raceId=rs.raceId
  WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2008 AND 2017
)
SELECT raceId, year, points, rn, cnt FROM racept LIMIT 5

WITH racept AS (
  SELECT rs.raceId,
         rs.points,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY rs.raceId ORDER BY rs.points) AS rn,
         COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY rs.raceId) AS cnt
  FROM results rs
  WHERE rs.raceId IN (SELECT raceId FROM races WHERE year BETWEEN 2008 AND 2017)
),
median AS (
  SELECT raceId, AVG(points) AS median_points
  FROM racept
  WHERE rn IN ((cnt+1)/2, (cnt+2)/2)
  GROUP BY raceId
),
winner AS (
  SELECT rs.raceId, rs.driverId, rs.points AS winner_points
  FROM results rs
  WHERE rs.positionOrder = 1
    AND rs.raceId IN (SELECT raceId FROM races WHERE year BETWEEN 2008 AND 2017)
),
rcount AS (
  SELECT rs.raceId, COUNT(*) AS cnt
  FROM results rs
  WHERE rs.raceId IN (SELECT raceId FROM races WHERE year BETWEEN 2008 AND 2017)
  GROUP BY rs.raceId
)
SELECT r.year, r.name, d.forename, d.surname,
       w.winner_points, m.median_points,
       ROUND(w.winner_points - m.median_points, 3) AS gap,
       c.cnt
FROM winner w
JOIN median m ON w.raceId = m.raceId
JOIN rcount c ON w.raceId = c.raceId
JOIN races r ON w.raceId = r.raceId
JOIN drivers d ON w.driverId = d.driverId
WHERE c.cnt >= 10
ORDER BY gap DESC

case.name: advanced_024
case.question: Which five drivers increased their points per race by the largest percentage from 2008 to 2017, considering only drivers who scored points in both years? Report both race counts, both rates, and absolute and percentage growth.
case.reference_answer: The results were: driver: Sebastian Vettel, 2008 races: 18, 2017 races: 20, 2008 points per race: 1.944, 2017 points per race: 15.85, absolute growth: 13.906, percentage growth: 715.14; driver: Lewis Hamilton, 2008 races: 18, 2017 races: 20, 2008 points per race: 5.444, 2017 points per race: 18.15, absolute growth: 12.706, percentage growth: 233.37; driver: Kimi R�_ikk̦nen, 2008 races: 18, 2017 races: 20, 2008 points per race: 4.167, 2017 points per race: 10.25, absolute growth: 6.083, percentage growth: 146.0; driver: Felipe Massa, 2008 races: 18, 2017 races: 19, 2008 points per race: 5.389, 2017 points per race: 2.263, absolute growth: -3.126, percentage growth: -58.0; driver: Fernando Alonso, 2008 races: 18, 2017 races: 19, 2008 points per race: 3.389, 2017 points per race: 0.895, absolute growth: -2.494, percentage growth: -73.6.
case.gold_sql:
WITH yearly AS (
  SELECT res.driverId, r.year,
         COUNT(DISTINCT res.raceId) AS races,
         SUM(res.points) AS points
  FROM results AS res
  JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId
  WHERE r.year IN (2008, 2017)
  GROUP BY res.driverId, r.year
), paired AS (
  SELECT y08.driverId,
         y08.races AS races_2008, y17.races AS races_2017,
         y08.points AS points_2008, y17.points AS points_2017,
         y08.points / y08.races AS ppr_2008,
         y17.points / y17.races AS ppr_2017
  FROM yearly AS y08
  JOIN yearly AS y17 ON y17.driverId = y08.driverId AND y17.year = 2017
  WHERE y08.year = 2008 AND y08.points > 0 AND y17.points > 0
)
SELECT d.forename || ' ' || d.surname AS driver,
       races_2008, races_2017,
       ROUND(ppr_2008, 3) AS points_per_race_2008,
       ROUND(ppr_2017, 3) AS points_per_race_2017,
       ROUND(ppr_2017 - ppr_2008, 3) AS absolute_growth,
       ROUND(100.0 * (ppr_2017 - ppr_2008) / ppr_2008, 2) AS percentage_growth
FROM paired AS p
JOIN drivers AS d ON d.driverId = p.driverId
ORDER BY percentage_growth DESC, absolute_growth DESC
LIMIT 5

SELECT c.name AS constructor,

FROM results AS res
JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId
JOIN constructors AS c ON c.constructorId = res.constructorId

WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2010 AND 2017
GROUP BY res.constructorId, res.driverId, c.name, d.forename, d.surname

ORDER BY win_rate DESC, wins DESC, starts DESC

case.name: advanced_026
case.question: Which five seasons from 2008-2017 had the largest gap between the leading constructor's points and the median constructor's points? Report the leading constructor, leader points, median points, and gap.
case.reference_answer: The results were: year: 2016, leading constructor: Mercedes, leader points: 765.0, median points: 76.0, gap: 689.0; year: 2015, leading constructor: Mercedes, leader points: 703.0, median points: 78.0, gap: 625.0; year: 2017, leading constructor: Mercedes, leader points: 668.0, median points: 70.0, gap: 598.0; year: 2011, leading constructor: Red Bull, leader points: 650.0, median points: 56.5, gap: 593.5; year: 2014, leading constructor: Mercedes, leader points: 701.0, median points: 155.0, gap: 546.0.
case.gold_sql:
WITH constructor_points AS (
  SELECT r.year, cr.constructorId, SUM(cr.points) AS points
  FROM constructorResults AS cr
  JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = cr.raceId
  WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2008 AND 2017
  GROUP BY r.year, cr.constructorId
), ranked AS (
  SELECT cp.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY year ORDER BY points) AS rn,
         COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY year) AS constructor_count,
         MAX(points) OVER (PARTITION BY year) AS leader_points,
         FIRST_VALUE(constructorId) OVER (PARTITION BY year ORDER BY points DESC, constructorId) AS leader_id
  FROM constructor_points AS cp
), season_stats AS (
  SELECT year, leader_id, leader_points,
         AVG(CASE WHEN rn IN ((constructor_count + 1) / 2, (constructor_count + 2) / 2) THEN points END) AS median_points
  FROM ranked
  GROUP BY year, leader_id, leader_points
)
SELECT s.year, c.name AS leading_constructor,
       ROUND(s.leader_points, 3) AS leader_points,
       ROUND(s.median_points, 3) AS median_points,
       ROUND(s.leader_points - s.median_points, 3) AS leader_median_gap
FROM season_stats AS s
JOIN constructors AS c ON c.constructorId = s.leader_id
ORDER BY leader_median_gap DESC, s.year
LIMIT 5

case.name: advanced_027
case.question: Which five long-career drivers were the most reliable from 2010-2017? Require at least 100 starts and 20 top-five finishes; report classified rate, retirements, and top-five rate.
case.reference_answer: The results were: driver: Sebastian Vettel, starts: 156, top-five finishes: 123, classified rate: 90.38, retirements: 15, top-five rate: 78.85; driver: Nico Rosberg, starts: 136, top-five finishes: 75, classified rate: 89.71, retirements: 14, top-five rate: 55.15; driver: Felipe Massa, starts: 155, top-five finishes: 41, classified rate: 89.03, retirements: 17, top-five rate: 26.45; driver: Lewis Hamilton, starts: 156, top-five finishes: 118, classified rate: 88.46, retirements: 18, top-five rate: 75.64; driver: Daniel Ricciardo, starts: 129, top-five finishes: 46, classified rate: 87.6, retirements: 16, top-five rate: 35.66.
case.gold_sql:
SELECT d.forename || ' ' || d.surname AS driver,
       COUNT(*) AS starts,
       SUM(CASE WHEN res.positionOrder <= 5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS top_five_finishes,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN res.positionText != 'R' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS classified_rate,
       SUM(CASE WHEN res.positionText = 'R' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS retirements,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN res.positionOrder <= 5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS top_five_rate
FROM results AS res
JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId
JOIN drivers AS d ON d.driverId = res.driverId
WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2010 AND 2017
GROUP BY res.driverId, d.forename, d.surname
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 100
   AND SUM(CASE WHEN res.positionOrder <= 5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) >= 20
ORDER BY classified_rate DESC, top_five_rate DESC
LIMIT 5

case.name: advanced_028
case.question: Which five constructors showed the smallest average points gap between their top two scoring drivers per race from 2014-2017? Require at least 30 races with two drivers; report the number of races and both gap measures.
case.reference_answer: The results were: constructor: Manor Marussia, races with two drivers: 39, average top-two points gap: 0.03, largest top-two points gap: 1.0; constructor: Sauber, races with two drivers: 79, average top-two points gap: 0.42, largest top-two points gap: 8.0; constructor: Renault, races with two drivers: 41, average top-two points gap: 1.59, largest top-two points gap: 8.0; constructor: Haas F1 Team, races with two drivers: 41, average top-two points gap: 1.71, largest top-two points gap: 10.0; constructor: Lotus F1, races with two drivers: 38, average top-two points gap: 2.0, largest top-two points gap: 15.0.
case.gold_sql:
WITH race_driver_points AS (
  SELECT res.constructorId, res.raceId, res.driverId, SUM(res.points) AS points
  FROM results AS res
  JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId
  WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2014 AND 2017
  GROUP BY res.constructorId, res.raceId, res.driverId
), ranked AS (
  SELECT rdp.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY constructorId, raceId ORDER BY points DESC, driverId) AS driver_rank,
         COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY constructorId, raceId) AS drivers_in_race
  FROM race_driver_points AS rdp
), teammate_gaps AS (
  SELECT constructorId, raceId,
         MAX(CASE WHEN driver_rank = 1 THEN points END) - MAX(CASE WHEN driver_rank = 2 THEN points END) AS points_gap
  FROM ranked
  WHERE drivers_in_race >= 2
  GROUP BY constructorId, raceId
)
SELECT c.name AS constructor,
       COUNT(*) AS races_with_two_drivers,
       ROUND(AVG(points_gap), 2) AS avg_top_two_points_gap,
       ROUND(MAX(points_gap), 2) AS largest_top_two_points_gap
FROM teammate_gaps AS tg
JOIN constructors AS c ON c.constructorId = tg.constructorId
GROUP BY tg.constructorId, c.name
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 30
ORDER BY avg_top_two_points_gap ASC, races_with_two_drivers DESC
LIMIT 5

SELECT r.year, res.raceId, res.constructorId, c.name AS constructor, res.driverId, d.surname AS driver, res.points, res.positionOrder
FROM results res
JOIN races r ON r.raceId=res.raceId
JOIN constructors c ON c.constructorId=res.constructorId
JOIN drivers d ON d.driverId=res.driverId
WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2014 AND 2017
ORDER BY res.raceId, res.constructorId, res.points DESC
LIMIT 50

WITH yearly AS (
  SELECT r.year, res.raceId, res.constructorId,
         res.driverId, res.points,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY r.year, res.constructorId, res.raceId ORDER BY res.points DESC) AS rk
  FROM results res
  JOIN races r ON r.raceId=res.raceId
  WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2014 AND 2017 AND res.points > 0
)
SELECT year, constructorId, COUNT(*) AS driversWithPts, COUNT(DISTINCT raceId) AS races
FROM yearly WHERE rk <= 2
GROUP BY year, constructorId
ORDER BY constructorId, year

WITH per_race AS (
  SELECT r.year, res.raceId, res.constructorId, res.driverId, res.points,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY res.raceId, res.constructorId ORDER BY res.points DESC, res.positionOrder ASC) AS rk
  FROM results res
  JOIN races r ON r.raceId=res.raceId
  WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2014 AND 2017 AND res.points > 0
),
rc AS (
  SELECT year, raceId, constructorId
  FROM per_race
  GROUP BY raceId, constructorId
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
)
SELECT per_race.constructorId, per_race.year, per_race.raceId, 
       MAX(CASE WHEN rk=1 THEN per_race.points END) AS p1,
       MAX(CASE WHEN rk=2 THEN per_race.points END) AS p2
FROM per_race
JOIN rc ON rc.raceId=per_race.raceId AND rc.constructorId=per_race.constructorId
WHERE per_race.rk <= 2
GROUP BY per_race.raceId, per_race.constructorId
ORDER BY per_race.constructorId, per_race.year, per_race.raceId

case.gold_sql: SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS starts, ROUND(AVG(res.grid - res.positionOrder), 3) AS average_gain FROM results AS res JOIN constructors AS c ON c.constructorId = res.constructorId JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2013 AND 2017 AND res.grid > 0 GROUP BY c.constructorId, c.name HAVING COUNT(*) >= 100 ORDER BY average_gain DESC, starts DESC, c.name LIMIT 5

result.answer:
All nine constructors with at least 100 starts are represented in that period, and the five that gained the most grid positions on average (i.e., highest average of finishing position minus starting grid) are as follows.

Based on the data in the database (races from 2013–2017, counting each constructor's classified finishes where final position is available and grid ≥ 1):

**The five constructors who gained the most grid positions on average (2013–2017, ≥100 starts):**

1. **Sauber** – +1.015 positions gained on average (195 finishes)
2. **McLaren** – +0.388 positions gained on average (196 finishes)
3. **Force India** – +0.158 positions gained on average (196 finishes)
4. **Lotus F1** – –0.184 positions gained on average (114 finishes)
5. **Williams** – –0.328 positions gained on average (195 finishes)

Notes/qualifiers:
- "Grid positions gained" is computed as the finishing order position subtracted from the starting grid position, averaged over races where the driver had a classified finish.
- All nine constructors competing in that window had at least 100 starts, so the top five are simply the five with the highest average gain.
- Only Sauber and McLaren, on average, actually *gained* grid positions (positive gains); the remainder of the qualifying field, including Lotus F1 and Williams, had negative averages (i.e., they tended to lose positions on average).

sql_attempts.query:
SELECT c.name, 
       COUNT(*) as num_starts,
       AVG(r.grid - r.positionOrder) as avg_grid_gain
FROM results r
JOIN races ra ON r.raceId = ra.raceId
JOIN constructors c ON r.constructorId = c.constructorId
WHERE ra.year BETWEEN 2013 AND 2017
  AND r.grid >= 1
  AND r.positionOrder > 0
GROUP BY c.constructorId, c.name
HAVING num_starts >= 100
ORDER BY avg_grid_gain DESC
LIMIT 10

sql_attempts.query:
WITH cte AS (
  SELECT r.constructorId, d.forename || ' ' || d.surname AS driver_name,
         SUM(r.points) AS driver_points
  FROM results r
  JOIN races rc ON rc.raceId = r.raceId
  JOIN drivers d ON d.driverId = r.driverId
  WHERE rc.year = 2017
  GROUP BY r.constructorId, r.driverId
),
team_totals AS (
  SELECT r.constructorId, SUM(r.points) AS team_total
  FROM results r
  JOIN races rc ON rc.raceId = r.raceId
  WHERE rc.year = 2017
  GROUP BY r.constructorId
)
SELECT team_totals.constructorId, c.name,
       cte.driver_name, cte.driver_points,
       team_totals.team_total,
       cte.driver_points / team_totals.team_total AS share
FROM team_totals
JOIN cte ON cte.constructorId = team_totals.constructorId
JOIN constructors c ON c.constructorId = team_totals.constructorId
WHERE cte.driver_points = (
   SELECT MAX(driver_points) FROM cte WHERE cte.constructorId = team_totals.constructorId
)
ORDER BY share DESC

result.answer:
Let me verify these results against the data one more time and summarize the analysis.

Based on my analysis of the database, let me present the key findings.

I computed points-per-race (total constructor points ÷ number of races that season) for each constructor that competed in **both** 2015 and 2017 (2015 had 19 races, 2017 had 20 races).

The constructors present in both seasons and their changes in points per race:

| Constructor | 2015 PPR | 2017 PPR | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Red Bull | 9.84 | 18.40 | **+8.56** |
| Ferrari | 22.53 | 26.10 | **+3.57** |
| Force India | 7.16 | 9.35 | **+2.19** |
| McLaren | 1.42 | 1.50 | **+0.08** |
| Toro Rosso | 3.53 | 2.65 | −0.88 |
| Sauber | 1.89 | 0.25 | −1.64 |
| Mercedes | 37.00 | 33.40 | −3.60 |
| Williams | 13.53 | 4.15 | −9.38 |

**Important finding:** The question asks for *five* constructors that improved points per race, but the data shows that only **four** constructors (among those that competed in both seasons) actually *improved* their points per race from 2015 to 2017:

1. **Red Bull** (+8.56 points per race)
2. **Ferrari** (+3.57)
3. **Force India** (+2.19)
4. **McLaren** (+0.08)

The other persistent constructors (Toro Rosso, Sauber, Mercedes, Williams) all *declined* in points per race. Teams present in only one of the two years (e.g., Lotus F1/Renault, Haas, Manor/Marussia) cannot be compared across both seasons, and the Lotus→Renault lineage was also a decline (78 pts in 2015 → 57 pts in 2017).

So the data supports only **four** qualifying constructors, not five. If you needed a fifth by ranking the largest changes (including declines), Toro Rosso would be next at −0.88, but that was not an improvement. I'd recommend confirming whether the intended comparison uses different team-mapping or a different pair of seasons.

  SUM(CASE WHEN r.year=2015 THEN res.points ELSE 0 END) AS pts2015,

  SUM(CASE WHEN r.year=2017 THEN res.points ELSE 0 END) AS pts2017,

FROM results res

SELECT d.driverId, d.forename, d.surname,
  SUM(CASE WHEN r.year=2015 THEN res.points ELSE 0 END)/SUM(CASE WHEN r.year=2015 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS ppr2015,
  SUM(CASE WHEN r.year=2017 THEN res.points ELSE 0 END)/SUM(CASE WHEN r.year=2017 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS ppr2017,
  (SUM(CASE WHEN r.year=2017 THEN res.points ELSE 0 END)/SUM(CASE WHEN r.year=2017 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)) -
  (SUM(CASE WHEN r.year=2015 THEN res.points ELSE 0 END)/SUM(CASE WHEN r.year=2015 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)) AS improvement
FROM results res
JOIN races r ON res.raceId = r.raceId
JOIN drivers d ON res.driverId = d.driverId
WHERE r.year IN (2015, 2017)
GROUP BY d.driverId
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN r.year=2015 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) >= 10
   AND SUM(CASE WHEN r.year=2017 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) >= 10
ORDER BY improvement DESC

case.question: Which five constructors had the highest 2017 top-ten finishing rate with at least 10 entries?
case.reference_answer: The ranked rates were: (Mercedes, 40, 39, 97.5); (Force India, 40, 35, 87.5); (Ferrari, 40, 34, 85); (Red Bull, 40, 27, 67.5); (Williams, 40, 20, 50).
case.gold_sql: SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS entries, SUM(CASE WHEN res.positionOrder <= 10 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS top_ten, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN res.positionOrder <= 10 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS top_ten_pct FROM results AS res JOIN constructors AS c ON c.constructorId = res.constructorId JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId WHERE r.year = 2017 GROUP BY c.constructorId, c.name HAVING COUNT(*) >= 10 ORDER BY top_ten_pct DESC, c.name LIMIT 5

result.answer:
There are 400 total results in 2017, consistent with 20 races × 20 cars. The data confirms the answer.

Based on the retrieved data, here are the five constructors with the highest 2017 top-ten finishing rate among those with at least 10 entries:

| Rank | Constructor | Entries | Top-10 Finishes | Rate |
|------|------------|---------|----------------|------|
| 1 | **Mercedes** | 40 | 39 | 97.5% |
| 2 | **Force India** | 40 | 35 | 87.5% |
| 3 | **Ferrari** | 40 | 34 | 85.0% |
| 4 | **Red Bull** | 40 | 27 | 67.5% |
| 5 | **Williams** | 40 | 20 | 50.0% |

All five constructors had 40 entries each (matching 20 races in 2017 × 2 cars), which exceeds the minimum of 10 entries. The top-ten finishing rate is computed as the number of race entries where the driver finished in position 10 or better, divided by the total number of entries for that constructor.

       SUM(CASE WHEN r.positionOrder <= 10 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as top_ten

JOIN constructors c ON r.constructorId = c.constructorId
WHERE ra.year = 2017
GROUP BY c.constructorId, c.name
HAVING total_entries >= 10
ORDER BY (SUM(CASE WHEN r.positionOrder <= 10 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 1.0 / COUNT(*)) DESC
LIMIT 5

JOIN constructors c ON r.constructorId = c.constructorId
WHERE ra.year = 2017

case.question: Which five constructors had the highest rate of wins started from pole from 2008 through 2017?
case.reference_answer: The ranked rates were: (Toro Rosso, 1, 1, 100); (Mercedes, 67, 46, 68.66); (Red Bull, 55, 29, 52.73); (Brawn, 8, 4, 50); (Ferrari, 28, 9, 32.14).
case.gold_sql: SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS wins, SUM(CASE WHEN q.position = 1 AND res.grid = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pole_wins, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN q.position = 1 AND res.grid = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS pole_win_pct FROM results AS res JOIN constructors AS c ON c.constructorId = res.constructorId JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId LEFT JOIN qualifying AS q ON q.raceId = res.raceId AND q.driverId = res.driverId WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2008 AND 2017 AND res.position = '1' GROUP BY c.constructorId, c.name ORDER BY pole_win_pct DESC, pole_wins DESC, c.name LIMIT 5

result.answer:
I have the results. Let me present the answer with a clear definition of the metric I used.

I defined the **rate of wins started from pole** as the proportion of a constructor's race wins (2008–2017) in which the winning driver started from pole (grid position 1), i.e., *pole wins ÷ total wins*.

Here are the top five constructors by that rate (from the 2008–2017 data):

| Rank | Constructor | Wins from pole | Total wins | Rate |
|------|------------|----------------|------------|------|
| 1 | Williams | 1 | 1 | 100% |
| 2 | Toro Rosso | 1 | 1 | 100% |
| 3 | Mercedes | 46 | 67 | 68.7% |
| 4 | Red Bull | 30 | 55 | 54.5% |
| 5 | Brawn | 4 | 8 | 50.0% |

(For comparison: Ferrari was next at 32.1%, McLaren at 30.8%.)

Note: The two top-rated entries — Williams (1/1) and Toro Rosso (1/1) — each won only a single race in this period, so their 100% rates are based on very small samples. Among constructors with a more substantial number of wins, Mercedes had the highest pole-to-win share (68.7%).

case.reference_answer: The comparison results were: (before_2000, 185, 649, 28.51); (from_2000, 220, 330, 66.67).
case.gold_sql: WITH periods AS (SELECT CASE WHEN r.year < 2000 THEN 'before_2000' ELSE 'from_2000' END AS period, res.driverId, COUNT(*) AS wins FROM results AS res JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId WHERE res.position = '1' GROUP BY period, res.driverId), totals AS (SELECT period, SUM(wins) AS all_wins FROM periods GROUP BY period), top AS (SELECT period, SUM(wins) AS top_wins FROM (SELECT period, wins, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY period ORDER BY wins DESC, driverId) AS rank FROM periods) WHERE rank <= 5 GROUP BY period) SELECT top.period, top.top_wins, totals.all_wins, ROUND(100.0 * top.top_wins / totals.all_wins, 2) AS share_pct FROM top JOIN totals ON totals.period = top.period ORDER BY top.period

## Answer

I analyzed race wins in this Formula 1 database (covering 1950–2018). Here "top five drivers" refers to the five winningest drivers within each era, and treated "before 2000" as years **< 2000** and "after 2000" as years **> 2000**, with the turn-of-year races in 2000 excluded from both groups.

### Before 2000 (years < 2000)
- Total race wins: **649**
- Top-five drivers by wins: Alain Prost (51), Ayrton Senna (41), Michael Schumacher (35), Nigel Mansell (31), Jackie Stewart (27)
- Combined top-five wins: **185**
- **Top-five share: 185 / 649 ≈ 28.5%**

### After 2000 (years > 2000)
- Total race wins: **313**
- Top-five drivers by wins: Lewis Hamilton (62), Michael Schumacher (47), Sebastian Vettel (47), Fernando Alonso (32), Nico Rosberg (23)
- Combined top-five wins: **211**
- **Top-five share: 211 / 313 ≈ 67.4%**

### Conclusion
The share of race wins taken by the top five drivers **rose dramatically** from **≈28.5% before 2000 to ≈67.4% after 2000**. In other words, race victories became far more concentrated among the sport's top drivers in the post-2000 era than they were in the earlier decades covered by this database.

Note: This is based on race wins counted from the `results` data (positionOrder = 1) joined to `races` by year. I treated the data as-is; year 2000 itself was excluded from both comparisons since the wording distinguished strictly "before" and "after" 2000.

case.reference_answer: The comparison results were: (before_2010, 11.219); (from_2010, 11.57).
case.gold_sql: SELECT CASE WHEN r.year < 2010 THEN 'before_2010' ELSE 'from_2010' END AS period, ROUND(AVG(res.grid), 3) AS average_grid FROM results AS res JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId GROUP BY period ORDER BY period

result.answer:
I now have the data needed to answer the question.

## Answer

Based on the database (covering F1 races from 1950–2018), here is how the average grid position changed around 2010:

Using actual starting grid positions (where `grid > 0`, excluding the 0-value entries which do not represent real starting slots):

| Period | Average Grid Position | Sample Size |
|--------|----------------------|-------------|
| **Before 2010** (1950–2009) | **12.15** | 18,767 |
| **2010 and after** (2010–2018) | **11.61** | 3,444 |

**Conclusion:** The average grid position *improved* after 2010 — it fell from **12.15** before 2010 to **11.61** in 2010 and after. Lower average grid numbers mean drivers started, on average, closer to the front of the pack in the post-2010 era than in the pre-2010 era.

Note on data quality: These figures exclude the `grid = 0` entries (1,553 before 2010, but only 13 after 2010), which do not correspond to actual starting positions. If those zero entries are included as-is, the pre-2010 average drops (to ~11.22), which would change the comparison — but since grid=0 does not represent a genuine grid slot, excluding them gives the more meaningful comparison above.

SELECT r.year, s.status, COUNT(*) as cnt
FROM results res
JOIN races r ON res.raceId = r.raceId
JOIN status s ON res.statusId = s.statusId
WHERE r.year BETWEEN 2008 AND 2012
GROUP BY r.year, s.status
ORDER BY r.year, cnt DESC

  r.year,
  COUNT(*) as total_starts,
  SUM(CASE WHEN s.status <> 'Finished' AND s.status NOT LIKE '+%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as retirements
FROM results res

JOIN status s ON res.statusId = s.statusId

case.question: How did pole-to-win conversion change before and after 2010?
case.reference_answer: The comparison results were: (before_2010, 189, 91, 48.15); (from_2010, 156, 80, 51.28).
case.gold_sql: SELECT CASE WHEN r.year < 2010 THEN 'before_2010' ELSE 'from_2010' END AS period, COUNT(*) AS poles, SUM(CASE WHEN res.position = '1' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS wins, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN res.position = '1' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS conversion_pct FROM qualifying AS q JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = q.raceId JOIN results AS res ON res.raceId = q.raceId AND res.driverId = q.driverId WHERE q.position = 1 GROUP BY period ORDER BY period

result.answer:
I've reached the query limit. Let me work with the data I already have.

Let me also reconsider the winner counts. Earlier query returned before_2010 winner rows = 823 and after = 156 (distinct would be slightly less due to duplicate winner rows). But my robust "pole-won" distinct race counts were 328 before and 82 after, using distinct race IDs.

Let me reconcile denominators. The cleanest measure uses distinct race counts. Let me reconsider the earlier data points I gathered reliably:

From my queries, these are confirmed:
- Total races in DB: before 2010 = **820**, after 2010 = **177** (min year 1950, max 2018).
- Races with pole (grid=1) data: before = 820, after = **156** (all 21 missing ones were 2018 incomplete season).
- Pole-to-win (winner from pole, distinct races): before = **328**, after = **82**.

I can now compute the conversion rates.

For **before 2010**: all 820 races have pole data, pole-sitter won 328 times → **328/820 = 40.0%**

For **after 2010**: among the 156 races (2010–2017) with pole data, pole-sitter won 82 times → **82/156 = 52.6%**

(If we used all 177 after-2010 races, the 2018 races lack data, so the 156-race denominator with full data is the appropriate basis.)

---

## Summary

Based on data retrieved from the F1 results database (spanning 1950–2018, with the 2018 season's results/grid data incomplete):

**Pole-to-win conversion** (the rate at which the pole-sitter goes on to win the race):

| Period | Races analyzed | Winner from pole | Conversion rate |
|--------|----------------|------------------|-----------------|
| **Before 2010** (1950–2009) | 820 | 328 | **40.0%** |
| **After 2010** (2010–2017) | 156 | 82 | **52.6%** |

**Key finding:** Pole-to-win conversion **increased** after 2010, rising from **40.0%** before 2010 to **52.6%** after 2010 — an improvement of roughly 12.6 percentage points.

Notes on data caveats:
- The 2018 season (21 races) lacked grid/pole data in the database, so the "after 2010" analysis covers 2010–2017 only.
- A few races in the early 1950s had duplicate data records, but these were handled by counting distinct races and do not materially affect the results.

All figures above are derived solely from the database query results.

sql_attempts.query:
SELECT 
  CASE WHEN r.year < 2010 THEN 'before_2010' ELSE 'after_2010' END AS period,
  COUNT(*) AS total_races_with_pole,
  SUM(CASE WHEN res.grid = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pole_wins
FROM races r
JOIN results res ON res.raceId = r.raceId
WHERE res.grid = 1 AND res.positionOrder = 1
GROUP BY period

SELECT 
  CASE WHEN r.year < 2010 THEN 'before_2010' ELSE 'after_2010' END AS period,
  COUNT(*) AS num_races,
  SUM(CASE WHEN res.positionOrder = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pole_to_win
FROM races r
JOIN results res ON res.raceId = r.raceId AND res.grid = 1
WHERE res.position IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY period

SELECT 
  CASE WHEN r.year < 2010 THEN 'before' ELSE 'after' END AS period,
  COUNT(DISTINCT r.raceId) AS total_races
FROM races r
GROUP BY period
SELECT MIN(year), MAX(year) FROM races

SELECT 
  CASE WHEN r.year < 2010 THEN 'before_2010' ELSE 'after_2010' END AS period,
  COUNT(*) AS num_pole_slot_results
FROM races r
JOIN results res ON res.raceId = r.raceId AND res.grid = 1
GROUP BY period

SELECT 
  CASE WHEN r.year < 2010 THEN 'before_2010' ELSE 'after_2010' END AS period,
  COUNT(*) AS total_races,
  SUM(CASE WHEN win.grid = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS winner_from_pole
FROM races r
JOIN results win ON win.raceId = r.raceId AND win.positionOrder = 1
GROUP BY period

SELECT r.raceId, r.year, COUNT(*) AS winner_rows
FROM races r
JOIN results win ON win.raceId = r.raceId AND win.positionOrder = 1
GROUP BY r.raceId, r.year
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
LIMIT 20

SELECT 
  CASE WHEN r.year < 2010 THEN 'before_2010' ELSE 'after_2010' END AS period,
  COUNT(DISTINCT r.raceId) AS races_with_pole_result
FROM races r
JOIN results res ON res.raceId = r.raceId AND res.grid = 1
GROUP BY period

SELECT 
  CASE WHEN r.year < 2010 THEN 'before_2010' ELSE 'after_2010' END AS period,
  COUNT(DISTINCT r.raceId) AS races_where_pole_won
FROM races r
JOIN results pole ON pole.raceId = r.raceId AND pole.grid = 1
JOIN results win ON win.raceId = r.raceId AND win.positionOrder = 1 AND win.driverId = pole.driverId
GROUP BY period

SELECT r.raceId, r.year, r.name, COUNT(*) AS cn
FROM races r
LEFT JOIN results res ON res.raceId = r.raceId AND res.grid = 1
WHERE r.year >= 2010
GROUP BY r.raceId
HAVING COUNT(res.resultId) = 0

case.name: advanced_069
case.question: Which five constructors changed their race participation the most between 2014 and 2017?
case.reference_answer: The comparison results were: (Ferrari, 19, 20, 1); (Force India, 19, 20, 1); (McLaren, 19, 20, 1); (Mercedes, 19, 20, 1); (Red Bull, 19, 20, 1).
case.gold_sql: WITH counts AS (SELECT cr.constructorId, r.year, COUNT(DISTINCT cr.raceId) AS races FROM constructorResults AS cr JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = cr.raceId WHERE r.year IN (2014, 2017) GROUP BY cr.constructorId, r.year), paired AS (SELECT a.constructorId, a.races AS races_2014, b.races AS races_2017, b.races - a.races AS change FROM counts AS a JOIN counts AS b ON b.constructorId = a.constructorId WHERE a.year = 2014 AND b.year = 2017) SELECT c.name, races_2014, races_2017, change FROM paired JOIN constructors AS c ON c.constructorId = paired.constructorId ORDER BY ABS(change) DESC, c.name LIMIT 5
