I now have a clear dataset. Let me organize the full picture of race participation for every constructor appearing in either 2014 or 2017:

| Constructor | 2014 participation | 2017 participation | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Renault | 0 (not present) | 20 | +20 |
| Haas F1 Team | 0 (not present) | 20 | +20 |
| Lotus F1 | 19 | 0 (not present) | −19 |
| Caterham | 17 | 0 (not present) | −17 |
| Marussia | 16 | 0 (not present) | −16 |
| Williams/McLaren/Mercedes/Ferrari/Red Bull/Toro Rosso/Sauber/Force India | 19 | 20 | +1 each |

The eight constructors that participated in **both** 2014 and 2017 (McLaren, Mercedes, Ferrari, Red Bull, Williams, Force India, Sauber, Toro Rosso) all ran full seasons in each year — 19 of 19 races in 2014 and 20 of 20 races in 2017. Because the 2017 calendar simply had one more round than 2014, each of those teams changed their race participation by exactly the same amount (+1). The difference across those teams is purely the calendar length, not a change in team behavior.

The teams whose race participation actually changed the **most** between 2014 and 2017 are the ones whose participation wasn't constant—those that entered or left the grid:

1. **Renault** — from 0 races in 2014 to 20 in 2017 (joined/expanded) — change of **+20**
2. **Haas F1 Team** — from 0 races in 2014 to 20 in 2017 (new team) — change of **+20**
3. **Lotus F1** — from 19 races in 2014 to 0 in 2017 (left) — change of **−19**
4. **Caterham** — from 17 races in 2014 to 0 in 2017 (left) — change of **−17**
5. **Marussia** — from 16 races in 2014 to 0 in 2017 (left) — change of **−16**

So the five constructors whose race participation changed the most between 2014 and 2017 are **Renault, Haas F1 Team, Lotus F1, Caterham, and Marussia**.

**A note on interpretation:** All manufacturers that competed in *both* 2014 and 2017 (McLaren, Mercedes, Ferrari, Red Bull, Williams, Force India, Sauber, Toro Rosso) were full-season entrants both years, racing 19/19 rounds in 2014 and 20/20 in 2017. Their participation only differed by the one extra race on the 2017 calendar, so they all changed by the same small amount and none of them can be singled out as among the most-changed. The five above are the ones whose participant counts shifted the most, driven by entering or leaving the championship over that span.

SELECT c.name,
  SUM(CASE WHEN r.year=2014 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as cnt2014,
  SUM(CASE WHEN r.year=2017 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as cnt2017
FROM (
  SELECT DISTINCT res.constructorId, ra.year
  FROM results res
  JOIN races ra ON res.raceId=ra.raceId
  WHERE ra.year IN (2014,2017)
) x
JOIN constructors c ON c.constructorId=x.constructorId
JOIN (
  SELECT res.constructorId, ra.year, COUNT(DISTINCT res.raceId) as cnt
  FROM results res JOIN races ra ON res.raceId=ra.raceId
  WHERE ra.year IN (2014,2017)
  GROUP BY res.constructorId, ra.year
) t ON t.constructorId=x.constructorId AND t.year=x.year
GROUP BY c.name

SELECT c.name, x.year, COUNT(DISTINCT x.raceId) as participation
FROM (
  SELECT res.constructorId, res.raceId, ra.year
  FROM results res JOIN races ra ON res.raceId=ra.raceId
  WHERE ra.year IN (2014,2017)
) x
JOIN constructors c ON c.constructorId=x.constructorId
GROUP BY c.name, x.year
ORDER BY c.name, x.year

SELECT c.name,
  COALESCE(cnt2014,0) as p2014,
  COALESCE(cnt2017,0) as p2017,
  COALESCE(cnt2017,0)-COALESCE(cnt2014,0) as CHANGE
FROM (
  SELECT res.constructorId,
    SUM(CASE WHEN ra.year=2014 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) ... 
) -- placeholder

SELECT c.name,
  MAX(CASE WHEN yr.year=2014 THEN part.participation END) as p2014,
  MAX(CASE WHEN yr.year=2017 THEN part.participation END) as p2017
FROM (
  SELECT res.constructorId, ra.year, COUNT(DISTINCT res.raceId) as participation
  FROM results res JOIN races ra ON res.raceId=ra.raceId
  WHERE ra.year IN (2014,2017)
  GROUP BY res.constructorId, ra.year
) part
JOIN constructors c ON c.constructorId=part.constructorId
JOIN (SELECT 2014 as year UNION SELECT 2017 as year) yr ON yr.year=part.year
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY (COALESCE(MAX(CASE WHEN yr.year=2017 THEN part.participation END),0)-COALESCE(MAX(CASE WHEN yr.year=2014 THEN part.participation END),0)) DESC

case.name: advanced_086
case.question: Which five circuits had the highest average fastest-lap speed with at least 20 recorded results?
case.reference_answer: The cross-entity results were: (Autodromo Nazionale di Monza, 240.783, 289); (Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps, 224.268, 257); (Silverstone Circuit, 219.019, 287); (Red Bull Ring, 217.81, 79); (Istanbul Park, 215.231, 147).
case.gold_sql: SELECT ci.name, ROUND(AVG(res.fastestLapSpeed), 3) AS average_speed, COUNT(*) AS recorded FROM results AS res JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId JOIN circuits AS ci ON ci.circuitId = r.circuitId WHERE res.fastestLapSpeed IS NOT NULL AND res.fastestLapSpeed != '' GROUP BY ci.circuitId, ci.name HAVING COUNT(*) >= 20 ORDER BY average_speed DESC, ci.name LIMIT 5

| 1 | Autodromo Nazionale di Monza | ≈ 240.78 | 289 |

| 4 | Red Bull Ring | ≈ 217.81 | 79 |
| 5 | Istanbul Park | ≈ 215.23 | 147 |

These figures were computed by averaging the `fastestLapSpeed` values from the `results` table (joined to each circuit through the races) and filtering to circuits with at least 20 recorded fastest-lap speed entries. SELECT c.circuitId, c.name, 
       AVG(r.fastestLapSpeed) AS avg_speed,
       COUNT(r.fastestLapSpeed) AS num_results
FROM results r
JOIN races rc ON r.raceId = rc.raceId
JOIN circuits c ON rc.circuitId = c.circuitId
WHERE r.fastestLapSpeed IS NOT NULL AND r.fastestLapSpeed != ''
GROUP BY c.circuitId, c.name
HAVING COUNT(r.fastestLapSpeed) >= 20
ORDER BY avg_speed DESC
LIMIT 5

WITH race_fields AS (
  SELECT r.raceId, r.year, r.name, COUNT(*) AS field_size
  FROM results res
  JOIN races r ON r.raceId = res.raceId
  GROUP BY r.raceId
),
year_avg AS (
  SELECT year, AVG(field_size) AS year_avg_size
  FROM race_fields
  GROUP BY year
)
SELECT rf.name, rf.year, rf.field_size, ya.year_avg_size,
       rf.field_size * 1.0 / ya.year_avg_size AS ratio
FROM race_fields rf
JOIN year_avg ya ON ya.year = rf.year
ORDER BY ratio DESC
LIMIT 15;

case.gold_sql: WITH yearly AS (SELECT res.driverId, r.year, SUM(res.points) AS points FROM results AS res JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = res.raceId WHERE r.year IN (2016, 2017) GROUP BY res.driverId, r.year), paired AS (SELECT a.driverId, a.points AS points_2016, b.points AS points_2017, b.points - a.points AS change FROM yearly AS a JOIN yearly AS b ON b.driverId = a.driverId WHERE a.year = 2016 AND b.year = 2017) SELECT d.forename, d.surname, points_2016, points_2017, change FROM paired JOIN drivers AS d ON d.driverId = paired.driverId ORDER BY change, d.driverId LIMIT 5

case.gold_sql: WITH yearly AS (SELECT cr.constructorId, r.year, SUM(cr.points) AS points FROM constructorResults AS cr JOIN races AS r ON r.raceId = cr.raceId WHERE r.year IN (2016, 2017) GROUP BY cr.constructorId, r.year), paired AS (SELECT a.constructorId, a.points AS points_2016, b.points AS points_2017, b.points - a.points AS change FROM yearly AS a JOIN yearly AS b ON b.constructorId = a.constructorId WHERE a.year = 2016 AND b.year = 2017) SELECT c.name, points_2016, points_2017, change FROM paired JOIN constructors AS c ON c.constructorId = paired.constructorId ORDER BY change, c.name LIMIT 5

result.answer:
The data confirms the five constructors with the largest drops in points from 2016 to 2017 (using final championship points after the last race of each season).

The five constructors with the largest point drops from 2016 to 2017 were:

1. **Red Bull**: 468 → 368 (drop of 100 points)
2. **Mercedes**: 765 → 668 (drop of 97 points)
3. **Williams**: 138 → 83 (drop of 55 points)
4. **McLaren**: 76 → 30 (drop of 46 points)
5. **Toro Rosso**: 63 → 53 (drop of 10 points)

These figures come from the final constructor championship standings (last race of each season) in 2016 compared to 2017.

SELECT c.name AS constructor, 
       r2016.year AS year_2016, cs2016.points AS points_2016,
       r2017.year AS year_2017, cs2017.points AS points_2017
FROM constructors c
JOIN constructorStandings cs2016 ON cs2016.constructorId = c.constructorId
JOIN races r2016 ON r2016.raceId = cs2016.raceId AND r2016.year = 2016
JOIN constructorStandings cs2017 ON cs2017.constructorId = c.constructorId
JOIN races r2017 ON r2017.raceId = cs2017.raceId AND r2017.year = 2017
WHERE r2016.round = (SELECT MAX(round) FROM races WHERE year = 2016)
  AND r2017.round = (SELECT MAX(round) FROM races WHERE year = 2017)

SELECT constructor, points_2016, points_2017, (points_2016 - points_2017) AS drop_points
FROM (
  SELECT c.name AS constructor, 
         cs2016.points AS points_2016, cs2017.points AS points_2017
  FROM constructors c
  JOIN constructorStandings cs2016 ON cs2016.constructorId = c.constructorId
  JOIN races r2016 ON r2016.raceId = cs2016.raceId AND r2016.year = 2016
  JOIN constructorStandings cs2017 ON cs2017.constructorId = c.constructorId
  JOIN races r2017 ON r2017.raceId = cs2017.raceId AND r2017.year = 2017
  WHERE r2016.round = (SELECT MAX(round) FROM races WHERE year = 2016)
    AND r2017.round = (SELECT MAX(round) FROM races WHERE year = 2017)
)
ORDER BY drop_points DESC

case.question: Which five drivers had the widest range between their best and worst finishes with at least 50 starts?
case.reference_answer: The drivers with the widest finish ranges were: (Stefan, Johansson, 103, 2, 37, 35); (Aguri, Suzuki, 88, 3, 38, 35); (Bertrand, Gachot, 84, 5, 39, 34); (Nicola, Larini, 75, 2, 36, 34); (Roberto, Moreno, 74, 2, 36, 34).
case.gold_sql: SELECT d.forename, d.surname, COUNT(*) AS starts, MIN(res.positionOrder) AS best_finish, MAX(res.positionOrder) AS worst_finish, MAX(res.positionOrder) - MIN(res.positionOrder) AS finish_range FROM results AS res JOIN drivers AS d ON d.driverId = res.driverId GROUP BY d.driverId, d.forename, d.surname HAVING COUNT(*) >= 50 ORDER BY finish_range DESC, starts DESC, d.driverId LIMIT 5

result.answer:
Based on the data in the database, here are the five drivers with the widest range between their best and worst finishes, among those with at least 50 starts.

I treated each entry in the `results` table as a "start," used `positionOrder` as the finishing position, calculated best = minimum finish position and worst = maximum finish position, then computed the range = worst − best, filtering to drivers with 50+ starts.

| Driver | Starts | Best Finish | Worst Finish | Range |
|--------|--------|-------------|--------------|-------|
| Stefan Johansson | 103 | 2 | 37 | 35 |
| Aguri Suzuki | 88 | 3 | 38 | 35 |
| Bertrand Gachot | 84 | 5 | 39 | 34 |
| Nicola Larini | 75 | 2 | 36 | 34 |
| Roberto Moreno | 74 | 2 | 36 | 34 |

**Top five by range:** Stefan Johansson (35), Aguri Suzuki (35), Bertrand Gachot (34), Nicola Larini (34), and Roberto Moreno (34).

Note on methodology: I counted every `results` row per driver as a "start," and used the `positionOrder` value as each finish. Because `positionOrder` includes late classifications for drivers who retired or were involved in incidents (often the full grid size), the "worst finish" numbers here are large—drivers whose careers often ended with non-finishes. A stricter definition that counted only classified/point-finishing races could yield a different ranking.

GROUP BY r.year
ORDER BY finished_share ASC

## Answer

The question "Who is the best driver in Formula 1?" is subjective, but based on the data available in this database (covering 1950–2018), the strongest statistical case points to **Michael Schumacher**.

Here's what the database shows for the leading candidates:

**Michael Schumacher** dominates the key "greatest ever" metrics:
- **Most race wins ever: 91** (well ahead of anyone else)
- **Most World Championships: 7** (more than any other driver in the database)
- Win rate of ~29.6% across his 308 races

**Lewis Hamilton** (whose career extends beyond this database's 2018 cutoff) shows the strongest *per-race efficiency* among modern-era drivers still racing, with **62 wins** and a **~29.8% win rate** — the best win percentage of any driver with substantial modern-era participation.

Other historically significant figures in the data include:
- **Juan Manuel Fangio** — 5 championships and the **highest win rate of all (41.4%)**
- **Alain Prost** (51 wins, 4 championships), **Sebastian Vettel** (47 wins, 4 championships), and **Ayrton Senna** (41 wins, 3 championships)

**In summary:** Based on this database's records, no single driver tops every category. If you weight total wins and championship titles most heavily, **Michael Schumacher** (91 wins, 7 titles) stands out as the most statistically dominant. If you judge by *championship efficiency* in an era with far fewer races, **Juan Manuel Fangio** (5 titles from a small number of seasons, with a 41% win rate) also has a very strong claim.

Note: As a caveat, "best" is a matter of opinion, and these records reflect only up to the 2018 season contained in this database.
